template: Wald 95% confidence intervals can be too narrow when the random-effect group has few levels (this fit: `{group_name}` has {n_groups} levels, below the ~10-level rule of thumb). Consider `symbolize(fit, ci_method = "profile")` for honest asymmetric intervals, or wait on Satterthwaite / Kenward-Roger support in drmTMB (see drmTMB issue #317).
Wald confidence intervals are an asymptotic approximation. With n = {n_obs} observations the approximation is usually fine, but consider `ci_method = "profile"` if any band looks suspicious.

This fit attaches a phylogenetic correlation matrix A on the `{group_name}` random effect. The variance component sigma_p^2 is the across-species shared-evolutionary-history variance. metadata$phylo_representation = {phylo_representation}. See `sym$assumptions` for the stated and implied prior assumptions (Brownian motion, ultrametricity, branch-length scale).

glmmTMB::propto() attaches sigma_p^2 * A on the `{group_name}` block but also keeps an independent sigma_res^2 * I residual unless dispformula = ~ 0 is passed. The full conditional covariance is sigma_p^2 * A + sigma_res^2 * I -- two free scalars, not one. For Sigma = A exactly, use metafor::rma.mv(V = 0 * diag(k), R = list(species = A)) or wait for glmmTMB::equalto(). (Williams et al. 2025)

Both a phylogenetic and a non-phylogenetic tier share the grouping column `{group_name}`. The variance components sigma_p^2 and sigma_sp^2 are weakly identified when phylogenetic signal (Pagel's lambda) is close to 0 or 1. Consider profiling lambda or fixing one tier. References: Hadfield & Nakagawa 2010; Mizuno et al. 2026 section 4.
A is near-singular (rank {rank} < k = {k}); polytomies and zero branch lengths can cause this. Add a small jitter (A + eps * diag(k), eps = 1e-6) or resolve the polytomy.
Tree tip labels and the `{group_name}` column do not match exactly: {n_missing_tips} species in the data but not the tree; {n_extra_tips} in the tree but not the data.

This fit attaches a spatial covariance matrix Omega on `{group_name}`; sigma_omega^2 is the magnitude of the spatial signal. See `sym$assumptions` for the kernel choice and range-parameter interpretation.

Factor `{factor_name}` uses {contrast_desc}, not the default treatment (dummy) coding. The coefficient table and any reference-level reading assume treatment coding, so the printed reference may be empty or misleading. For comparisons that respect the actual coding, use `group_means(sym)` and `group_contrasts(sym, by = "{factor_name}")`.
